cards.headline: Ebola cases exceed 12,000 in Democratic Republic of Congo

pages.text: Confirmed Ebola infections in the Democratic Republic of Congo have reached 12,021, with 5,904 deaths reported, according to government data. The outbreak, caused by the rare Bundibugyo species of the Ebola virus, is the second-largest on record and is spreading faster than the 2014-16 West African outbreak, which infected more than 28,600 people and killed more than 11,000. Officials expressed concern that this epidemic could surpass the West African outbreak's death toll if not contained soon. There are currently no approved vaccines or treatments for this specific strain of the virus. Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of people who are sick or have died from the disease. Containment requires identifying and treating patients in isolation, monitoring those exposed, and ensuring safe burials for the deceased.

The outbreak began in mid-May in the northeastern Ituri province and has since spread to eight of the country's 26 provinces. Response efforts face significant obstacles, including armed conflict, poor roads, and strained health services. Fighting between the army and the Convention pour la révolution populaire (CRP)—a rebel group founded by former warlord Thomas Lubanga—has disrupted monitoring and prevented teams from reaching some communities. On November 24, 2026, approximately a dozen people, including two World Health Organization (WHO) personnel and Congolese health officials, were evacuated to Bunia after being trapped for three days in a hospital in Akwe due to intense crossfire, according to WHO Ebola incident manager Dr. Catherine Smallwood. Additionally, mistrust and misinformation have kept some residents from seeking medical care. Data from Africa CDC shows that only 15 per cent of new cases currently come from contacts known to health authorities, suggesting many chains of transmission are being missed.

A Reuters analysis of satellite imagery suggested the official death toll may be largely underestimated in two of the hardest-hit areas, noting that fields of new graves widely outstrip previous years. Beyond the health crisis, UNICEF reported that the outbreak is increasing the vulnerability of women and girls to gender-based violence. In Bunia and at the Rwampara displacement site, movement restrictions intended to contain the virus have disrupted daily livelihoods and small-scale trading, leading to heightened financial precarity for many women. While Ebola cases have been detected in five countries, the Democratic Republic of Congo is currently the only country with active cases.

cards.headline: Arab nations condemn deadly drone attack on Kuwait facility

pages.text: A drone attack targeting a vital facility in Kuwait killed two Italian technicians and injured two other people, prompting widespread condemnation from Arab nations. The Kuwait Defense Ministry reported that falling debris from intercepted drones killed the two Italians working at an air defense surveillance station and injured a Kuwaiti national and a Pakistani national. The attack also caused unspecified material damage. Following the incident, flights on the air traffic corridor between Europe, the Gulf region, and Asia crossing Iraq toward the Gulf were redirected south amid reports that Kuwait's airspace was closed. The Kuwait military stated that a number of hostile Iranian drones were detected and intercepted in its airspace.

Saudi Arabia led a regional condemnation of the strike, with its Foreign Ministry holding Tehran responsible for the consequences of its continued attacks. The Saudi Foreign Ministry warned that continued Iranian attacks would lead to further tensions and instability, undermining international efforts to restore regional security. Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its solidarity with Kuwait and its support for measures to protect Kuwait's sovereignty. Other nations, including the UAE, Bahrain, Qatar, and Jordan, joined the condemnation, describing the attack as a violation of Kuwait's sovereignty and a threat to regional security. The UAE Foreign Ministry, via the Emirates News Agency (WAM), extended condolences to the victims' families and reaffirmed support for Kuwait's efforts to safeguard its stability. Gulf Cooperation Council Secretary-General Jasem Al-Budaiwi described the attack as a dangerous escalation threatening regional and international peace and security, holding Iran responsible and reaffirming the bloc's support for Kuwait's right to defend itself. Bahrain urged the UN Security Council to ensure Iran's compliance with Resolution 2817 and hold the country accountable for the attacks.

cards.headline: Two Italian technicians killed in strike on Kuwaiti facility

pages.text: Two Italian nationals died following a drone strike on a vital site in Kuwait, according to the Kuwaiti Army and Italy's foreign ministry. The victims, identified by the Italian news agency Ansa as men aged 36 and 65, were technicians working for Rheinmetall Italia, the Italian branch of the German arms manufacturing company. They were performing maintenance work on detection antennas for the Skyguard air-defense system at an air defence detection station used by the Kuwaiti Armed Forces when the explosion occurred. In addition to the two deaths, Kuwait's defence ministry reported that one Kuwaiti national and one Pakistani national were injured by falling shrapnel. Both the Kuwaiti and Italian governments have blamed Iran for the attack, though Tehran has denied responsibility.

Kuwait's Army described the incident as a result of “heinous Iranian aggression.” Italy's foreign minister stated that investigations indicated the drone used in the attack was manufactured in Iran, noting that Iranian proxies are known to conduct attacks in the region. Following the strike, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni expressed her deepest sorrow and condolences to the victims' families. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen also expressed sadness, stating that pressure must be increased on Iran to end attacks against its neighbors and Gulf partners. On November 26, 2026, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said he had expressed condolences to his Italian and Kuwaiti counterparts, adding that the incident looked “suspicious” and appeared like a “precooked recipe for war.” Araghchi stated that Tehran would work with Kuwait and Italy to determine the cause of the strike. However, Iranian armed forces spokesperson Abolfazl Shekarchi previously stated that no military or offensive operations had been conducted by Iran, and Iran has denied attacking Kuwaiti airspace.

The strike follows a period of increased tension in the Middle East. Kuwait, a US ally, has been frequently targeted by Iranian attacks since the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran in February. Just over a week prior to this incident, Kuwait reported repelling overnight Iranian drone attacks on an airbase hosting US forces, marking the first such strikes on the country in more than two months. The broader conflict began in late February when the US and Israel attacked Iran, leading to Iranian retaliations involving missiles and drones directed at Israel and Gulf Arab states that host US military personnel and assets. Recent exchanges of fire between the US and Iran, alongside a deadlock in negotiations, have raised fears of a major escalation in the war.

cards.headline: Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia's Jazan refinery kills one worker

pages.text: A Houthi attack on a refinery in Jazan, south-west Saudi Arabia, killed a Nepali worker and injured several others of different nationalities, according to the Saudi Energy Ministry. The facility, located on the Red Sea coast, was hit by a “hostile aerial projectile” that sparked a fire and led to the suspension of some operations. Emergency and technical teams began work immediately following the attack to conduct safety checks and a damage assessment. The Saudi Energy Ministry expressed condolences to the family of the deceased and stated that the injured workers are receiving medical care. On November 25, 2026, the Coalition to Restore Legitimacy in Yemen, which is fighting against Yemen's internationally recognized government, announced it had destroyed a ballistic missile launch platform in Yemen's Hodeidah port that was used in the attack. The coalition warned the Houthis that targeting civilian infrastructure and civilians would result in a firm military response.

The Jazan refinery is capable of processing up to 400,000 barrels of crude oil per day. The attack occurred amid a series of strikes by the Iran-backed Houthis, who control Hodeidah port on the Yemeni west coast. On November 25, 2026, the Houthis also reported attacking the ports of Jeddah and Jazan, while the coalition reported that a projectile fell at Jazan port causing minor damage but no civilian injuries. The militia also attempted strikes on the Kingdom’s western region and Jeddah Islamic Port on the same day. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree also stated the group attacked Riyadh's financial district in three phases. These developments follow intensified fighting since the Houthis captured strategic areas along Yemen's Red Sea coast in September, advancing toward the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key global shipping route for Gulf oil producers.

cards.headline: New Zealand ruling coalition lacks majority following final election results

pages.text: The incumbent right-wing coalition in New Zealand lacks a parliamentary majority following the release of final election results on November 27, 2026. To remain in power and avoid a new election, Prime Minister Christopher Luxon and the National Party must secure the support of the centrist newcomer Opportunity party. In the 130-seat parliament, 66 seats are required for a majority, but the National-led bloc currently holds 65 seats. The results were finalized after the electoral commission tallied nearly 485,000 “special votes,” which are ballots cast by citizens living overseas or voting outside their registered electorate. These special votes typically skew left, and the final tally saw the National Party drop two seats to 40. The National-led coalition includes the National Party, the populist New Zealand First party, and the libertarian Act party. The current seat counts for these groups are 40, 12, and 13, respectively.

The centrist Opportunity party, which secured seven seats, has been described as the election's kingmaker. Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong told reporters that her party will negotiate with National, though she noted that all options remain on the table. Wong stated that all seven parties in parliament are responsible for delivering a stable government. Prime Minister Luxon acknowledged that negotiations may be challenging and will take time, telling reporters, “Kiwis won't thank us for rushing to an agreement that falls apart or for sending them back to the polls.” A government led by the centre-left Labour Party is not considered possible, as that bloc would not have enough seats even if Opportunity supported them. Other seat counts include the Greens with 17 seats and Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests, with five seats. Labour secured 36 seats.

The election outcome was influenced by changes in three electorate seats following the special vote count. Labour won the Wairarapa seat from National by 81 votes and took Hamilton East from National by 173 votes. The Greens won Wellington Bays from Labour by 1,610 votes. If National applies for a recount and wins back at least one of those seats, it could return to power with a slim majority without needing the Opportunity party. New Zealand uses a mixed-member proportional voting system, where voters make two choices: one for a local constituency representative and one for a political party. This system means most governments are formed through coalitions. The election campaign was shaped by voter frustration regarding high unemployment and the cost of living.

cards.headline: German court rejects firearm permit revocations tied to AfD youth wing

pages.text: Germany’s top administrative court ruled that supporters of the former youth wing of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party cannot be deemed unfit to hold firearm permits based solely on their membership in that group at the time. The court upheld lower court rulings that overturned the revocation of permits for two men, stating that authorities must establish an organization is actually pursuing anti-constitutional aims rather than merely being suspected of doing so. Under Germany's Weapons Act, which includes some of the strictest firearms laws in Europe, authorities may deny or revoke permits if an individual is deemed unreliable, such as through links to groups pursuing anti-constitutional objectives.

The case involved two men whose permits were revoked after Bavaria’s domestic intelligence agency informed authorities in 2022 that they were connected to the state's branch of the Junge Alternative youth wing. That branch had been under observation for suspected extremist activities since 2019. While the Junge Alternative was designated as a confirmed extremist organization by Germany’s domestic intelligence agency in a 2023 assessment, the court ruled that this classification could not be applied retroactively to earlier administrative decisions. The dissolved youth wing has strongly rejected its extremist classification and challenged it in court, accusing the intelligence agency of election interference prior to key state votes.

cards.headline: Canada’s Supreme Court to rule on Quebec religious symbols ban

pages.text: Canada’s Supreme Court is scheduled to rule on November 27, 2026, regarding a legal challenge to Bill 21, a Quebec law that prohibits certain public officials from wearing religious symbols while on duty. The law currently bans public school teachers, police officers, and other specific public officials from wearing religious attire at work. This ruling will determine the constitutionality of the restrictions first introduced in Quebec in 2019. The scope of these restrictions was later expanded under Bill 94, which prohibited parents wearing religious symbols from volunteering at their children's schools.

The impact of these laws is illustrated by Navien Waly, a 45-year-old former finance professional who intended to begin a career as a specialised educator. Waly, who began wearing the hijab at age 40, says she can no longer perform the work she was trained for as long as she continues to wear the garment. Additionally, after a decade of volunteering at her children's schools for events such as bake sales and graduation committees, Waly received an email stating her presence was no longer welcome due to the restrictions in Bill 94. Waly stated that the email felt like a “slap in the face” and noted that she has never spoken about her religion.

cards.headline: At least 31 people killed in Cairo fuel truck fire

pages.text: At least 31 people died after a fuel truck overturned and ignited on a crowded highway in Cairo, Egypt, according to the health ministry. The fire broke out on November 25, 2026, on the Ring Road, a major highway connecting different parts of the capital, in the densely populated Waraq neighbourhood. State media reported that the truck, which was loaded with fuel, burst into flames and engulfed nearby vehicles after overturning. AFP footage showed a large fireball and thick black smoke rising above the area as motorists attempted to escape. While surrounding buildings appeared to escape the flames, images showed a scene of burned-out cars as firefighters worked to douse the wreckage.

Egyptian prosecutors announced the arrest of a man accused of causing the fire. The prosecution stated the man admitted to speeding when his car collided with the tanker, which caused his steering wheel to slip from his hands and his car to veer off course. When the car hit the truck, one of its tyres exploded, causing the tanker to overturn and resulting in a petrol leak that ignited the fire. The health ministry reported that 39 ambulances were sent to the scene and 15 people were taken to the hospital with injuries, including four people in critical condition. Egypt's public prosecutor has opened an investigation and stated that DNA tests are being conducted to identify victims who were badly burned.

cards.headline: Donald Trump adds Ukraine to warning against expanding war, diverging from joint NATO statement

pages.text: President Donald Trump modified a joint statement with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte to include Ukraine in a warning against expanding the war, a departure from the original text that directed the warning solely at Russia. On Nov. 26, Trump published a version of the statement on Truth Social that emphasized the importance of both Russia and Ukraine avoiding actions that intentionally or unintentionally expand the war. This revised wording differed from the official joint statement released following a Nov. 25 meeting at Trump's Mar-a-Lago residence in Florida, which had only emphasized the importance of Russia avoiding such actions. A NATO official, speaking on condition of anonymity to Politico, indicated that both leaders had agreed to the original statement before Trump unilaterally changed the wording.

The change in wording occurs as European leaders express concern regarding the geographical expansion of the conflict. Recent incidents include Russian airspace violations in Poland and a Ukrainian strike on a Russian warship in the Mediterranean Sea. On Nov. 26, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul separately warned against the war's expansion while reaffirming support for Ukraine. During the Nov. 25 meeting with Rutte, Trump and the NATO Secretary General discussed the war in Ukraine and the conflict in Iran. In a separate social media post on Nov. 26, Trump stated he had urged Russian President Vladimir Putin to end military aggression across Europe during a meeting in Shenzhen, China, and expressed optimism regarding a potential peace agreement between Ukraine and Russia. The White House did not respond to requests for comment from Politico.

cards.headline: Ukraine says it has no intention of spreading war to Libya

pages.text: Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga stated that Ukraine is not attempting to spread its war with Russia to Libyan shores following attacks on two Russian ships off the coast of Benghazi. Sybiga said in a post on X that he called his Libyan counterpart, Al-Taher Al-Baour, to explain that Ukraine's actions are directed only against Russian military objects serving Russia's war and not against Libya or the Libyan people. Sybiga added that Ukraine has no intention of extending the war against Ukraine to Libya or any other country and reaffirmed support for Libya's sovereignty, territorial integrity, and reunification efforts. On November 23, 2026, Kyiv claimed responsibility for attacks on two Russian ships—one of which was sunk—at the weekend off the coast of Libya.

The maritime attacks have raised concerns regarding political and security repercussions in Libya, which is divided between a UN-recognized government in Tripoli and a parallel administration in Benghazi. The eastern administration, led by Khalifa Haftar, maintains close military and strategic ties with Russia. Following the incident, the Tripoli authorities demanded explanations from Kyiv and denied having any understanding with Ukraine amid speculation regarding their possible role in the operations. Meanwhile, the eastern administration has called for an international investigation into an alleged Ukrainian military presence in Libya. The UN mission in Libya also condemned the attacks, calling for an independent investigation and urging respect for Libyan sovereignty.

cards.headline: UK net migration falls to 77,000 in year to June 2026

pages.text: Net migration to the United Kingdom fell to 77,000 in the year ending June 2026, according to figures from the Office for National Statistics and the Home Office. This represents the lowest level of net migration since 1997, excluding the years of the Covid pandemic. The 77,000 figure is the difference between an estimated 738,000 people who immigrated to the UK and 661,000 who emigrated during that period. This marks the first time net migration has been in the tens of thousands since a target set by David Cameron’s government in 2010 went unfulfilled.

The current figure reflects a 62% fall over the past 12 months from 204,000 in the year ending June 2025. Since the peak of 944,000 in the year ending March 2023, net migration has fallen by more than 90%. The ONS figures for the year ending June 2026 show a decrease from an estimated 171,000 in 2025. For comparison, annual net migration in 1997 was 48,000.

Immigration fell by 17% over the year to June 2026, driven by fewer non-EU citizens being granted permission to work, study, apply for asylum, or bring family members to the UK. The data indicates that Keir Starmer’s policies contributed to this decline by making care workers and some mid-skilled jobs ineligible for work visas, suspending family reunion for refugees, and toughening restrictions for universities sponsoring international students.

cards.headline: Report concludes Israel institutionalized torture of Palestinian prisoners to extract confessions

pages.text: Israel has institutionalized the use of torture to extract confessions from Palestinian prisoners, according to a report from the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel (PCATI). The report states that Israel sometimes documents abuse in official records or grants advanced approval for “special measures” during interrogations. Sari Bashi, the executive director of PCATI, said the Israeli legal system officially sanctions torture as a tool for extracting confessions, regardless of whether the confessions are true. This practice occurs as Israel moves to implement a new death penalty law that targets Palestinians, which the report describes as a racist measure. The report notes that the use of torture is particularly egregious given initiatives to impose the death penalty in Israel for the first time since 1962.

PCATI examined 42 cases in which Palestinians filed complaints regarding the use of torture by Shin Bet interrogators over the last decade. Shin Bet is Israel’s internal security service. Of those 42 cases, more than three-quarters of the complainants said they confessed after the use of “torture or other illegal methods.” Additionally, one in 10 provided incriminating statements about other people while under torture. In hundreds of testimonies, Palestinian detainees have described interrogations involving physical violence such as kicking and slapping, threats, sexual violence, being held in stress positions, and extreme sleep deprivation. Although Israel’s supreme court explicitly prohibited sleep deprivation as a deliberate interrogation method in a 1999 ruling, the report indicates the practice continues.

The PCATI report details the case of a Palestinian lawyer arrested in February 2019 who was subjected to extreme sleep deprivation. During an interrogation period lasting 27.5 days, or 660 hours, he was questioned for more than 552 hours. This averaged 20 hours of questioning per day, with one single session lasting nearly 48 hours. The remaining 108 hours of that period were spent attending detention hearings and traveling. The report suggests these practices risk leading to irreversible miscarriages of justice.

cards.headline: Son of Myanmar's Aung San Suu Kyi expresses relief after first phone call in five years

pages.text: Kim Aris, the son of Myanmar's former de facto head of government Aung San Suu Kyi, said he was relieved to hear his mother's voice for the first time in five years. Aris expressed concern regarding her condition following her transfer by the Myanmar military to house arrest at an undisclosed location, questioning if the gesture was genuine. Aris told Euronews' The World Conversation that for two or three years, the family had not known if she was alive. He had previously run a proof-of-life campaign, and the Red Cross had visited her to confirm she was alive.

The recorded and monitored call, which focused on family matters, was arranged after the Myanmar embassy in London contacted the British Foreign Office the week before it occurred. Aris, a British citizen, stated that while the military calls her current situation house arrest, she is not in her own home and has no access to media. He noted she had previously been held in solitary confinement in a prison in the capital, Naypyidaw, with contact limited to military or police personnel and military doctors.

Aris suggested the military is using the transfer to project an image of moderation and urged the international community to maintain pressure rather than re-engage. He stated the military continues to receive money and weaponry to suppress the population despite sanctions. The military seized power in February 2021, refusing to recognize the 2020 election results led by Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy. This coup triggered a civil war involving pro-democracy forces and ethnic armed groups. Aris said more than 4 million people are internally displaced and a further 2 million have fled abroad, partly due to military-introduced conscription laws.

cards.headline: US Senate passes permitting reform bill that advocates say threatens clean water protections

pages.text: The US Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) in a 62-33 vote, a move that advocates warn could weaken water pollution protections while attempting to accelerate energy and infrastructure projects. The bill is currently being debated in the House of Representatives. While supporters argue the legislation will hasten the transition to clean energy, opponents contend it provides industry with a way to bypass environmental regulations for fossil fuel projects and data centers. The bill includes support from Democratic Senator Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, who co-sponsored the legislation and stated it could lower emissions by 1.5 gigatons through 2040. However, more than 120 scientists have signed an open letter urging the House to reject the bill, and the NGO Oceana stated the legislation would roll back ocean and wildlife protections, potentially increasing offshore oil and gas drilling and threats to marine life.

BAAJA is a permitting reform bill designed to reduce the time federal agencies spend approving major projects, such as power lines, natural gas plants, fossil fuel pipelines, and data centers. Under the proposed law, environmental hurdles would become easier to clear: fewer projects would require a National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) review, the timeframe for environmental assessments would be shorter, the window to sue over approved projects would shrink, and consultation periods regarding impacts on endangered species would be shortened. Beyond these procedural changes, the bill includes provisions that would make it more difficult for states to implement water pollution protections, double the time between automatic reviews of water pollution permits, and reduce transparency regarding the types and levels of water pollution. The American Chemistry Council and American Petroleum Institute have expressed support for the bill.

More than 50 groups representing communities impacted by Pfas—often called “forever chemicals”—have opposed the bill, warning it would weaken mechanisms used to regulate the discharge of these chemicals. Emily Donovan, co-founder of the Clean Cape Fear advocacy group in Wilmington, North Carolina, stated the law would “put us in more danger,” noting that the local drinking, surface, and ground water is already polluted by discharge from a nearby Pfas factory. Additionally, several Native American organizations have condemned the bill, as it could lower barriers for oil, gas, and mining projects on public and tribal lands. Brad Campbell, CEO of the Conservation Law Foundation, characterized the legislation as a “one-way ratchet for fossil fuels” that could be used by administrations hostile to clean energy to fast-track fossil fuel development.

cards.headline: Federal judge rules Trump administration's deep-sea mining lease plans off Northern Mariana Islands violate Endangered Species Act

pages.text: A federal judge has ruled that the Trump administration's plans to lease sea-floor areas off the Northern Mariana Islands violated the Endangered Species Act (ESA). District judge Jill Aiko Otake found that the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS)—the agency providing expert opinions for the lease sales—and Howard Lutnick, in his capacity as head of the department overseeing the agency, failed to consider potential effects that could follow once the leases are issued. This decision follows a similar ruling regarding a proposed lease sale off American Samoa. The administration had planned to put the Northern Mariana Islands leases up for sale on 16 December 2026, though it remains unclear what will happen next following this ruling.

The ruling noted that while the leases would only authorize preliminary surveying activity, they might eventually allow leaseholders to mine the ocean floor. Judge Otake stated that the potential impact of such mining had not been addressed in the biodiversity assessment used to approve the lease sales. Opposition groups that filed the lawsuit expressed concerns that deep-sea mining could cause long-term damage to the ocean ecosystem, including potential impacts on sea turtles in the area. The US government has stated it intends to begin deep-sea mining to secure access to critical minerals and to counter China's growing influence over components essential for electronics.

Deep-sea mining is a controversial process that uses vacuum technology to suck up mineral nodules from muddy sediment. This method can remove organisms that grow on the nodules, such as corals and sponges, many of which cannot grow anywhere else. While some scientists have raised concerns that the practice could damage little-understood deep-ocean ecosystems, industry supporters argue that the environmental effects are uncertain and necessitate further study. Following a previous court ruling, the administration chose not to recognize the decision and proceeded with the sale of two leases covering 13 million hectares (more than 30 million acres) off American Samoa.

cards.headline: Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing rejects full compliance with ICJ genocide orders

pages.text: Myanmar's military-backed President, Min Aung Hlaing, stated his administration will not comply with all measures ordered by the International Court of Justice (ICJ). The ICJ, the United Nations' top court, recently ruled that Myanmar's security forces committed genocide against the mainly Muslim Rohingya minority. Min Aung Hlaing, who previously served as junta chief, rejected the verdict and said the term “genocide” has damaged the country's reputation. He told a meeting, according to state media, that while Myanmar would take actions appropriate for a responsible country, it would not comply with requirements it considers inappropriate, though he did not specify which orders were deemed inappropriate.

The ICJ ruling found that military actions against the Rohingya in 2017—which included thousands of killings, the burning of hundreds of villages, and widespread sexual violence—amounted to genocide. This marks the first instance of the UN court holding a state responsible for genocide. While the ruling is final, the ICJ has very limited options to enforce its decisions. Myanmar has maintained that its security force operations in northern Rakhine state during 2016–2018 were counter-terrorism actions against an insurgent group.

The ICJ ordered Myanmar to end ongoing breaches of the Genocide Convention and to investigate, prosecute, and punish people reasonably suspected of involvement in the 2017 military operations. The court also ordered the country to provide guarantees that such violations will not be repeated, facilitate the return of displaced Rohingya, restore or replace lost property, help locate missing people, provide rehabilitation to survivors, and protect the Rohingya from discrimination and persecution. Additionally, Myanmar must pay compensation for harm caused to the Rohingya that is not remedied through restitution. The court ordered Myanmar to report back within two years on the measures taken, including proposed compensation.

cards.headline: Ukraine targets Russian vessels in the Baltic and Mediterranean

pages.text: Ukraine has expanded its military operations beyond its borders by targeting Russian vessels in the Baltic and Mediterranean seas. These operations include an attack on the Russian cargo vessel Sparta II off the Finnish coast, as well as an attack on the Russian corvette Merkury and a dry cargo vessel, which was allegedly carrying weapons, off the coast of Libya. Kyiv is attempting to increase pressure on Moscow and signal its intentions to Western allies through these actions. Over the past few years, Ukraine has also used aerial and maritime drones to strike targets deep within Russian territory.

The escalation of maritime conflict follows an increase in attacks by both Russia and Ukraine in the Black Sea since the summer. In that region, targets have included Russian and Ukrainian cargo ships, as well as vessels from other nations, particularly Turkey. These developments occur amid warnings from intelligence agencies that Russia has been preparing provocations along NATO's eastern flank. Moscow has previously utilized military provocation, hybrid operations, and acts of sabotage to pressure countries that support Ukraine. These Ukrainian maritime operations follow incidents where several suspected Russian missiles crashed in Poland near an international military exercise.

cards.headline: Russian attacks kill 10 and injure 58 across Ukraine

pages.text: Russian attacks killed 10 people and injured 58 others, including three children, across Ukraine over the past day, according to local authorities. The strikes included a massive ballistic missile attack on Kyiv, where Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported that a shopping center was struck and seven people were injured. 113 drones—including 76 jet-powered models, Gerbera drones, and Parody decoys—along with an unspecified number of ballistic missiles, were launched at Ukraine overnight on Nov. 25, Ukraine's Air Force said. As of 8 a.m. local time, air defenses had downed or suppressed 87 drones, including 52 jet-powered ones. The Air Force recorded drone impacts at 20 locations and falling debris at six locations. In Kharkiv Oblast, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said Russia targeted Kharkiv and six other settlements, killing four people and injuring three others. The strikes hit an educational facility in Kharkiv and a farm building in Izyum. A married couple was killed in a strike on a multi-story apartment building in Kharkiv's Novobavarskyi District, and two people were killed on the road near the village of Dovzhyk. In Donetsk Oblast, Governor Vadym Filashkin reported that Russian attacks killed three people and injured 18. Specifically, two people were killed in Sloviansk and 12 others were injured by glide bombs and drone strikes. cards.headline: At least 16 schoolchildren killed in Gaza since start of November, ministry says

pages.text: Gaza’s ministry of education reported on November 25, 2026, that at least 16 schoolchildren have been killed in the Gaza Strip since the beginning of November. This follows a period of intensifying bombardment where young people in Gaza have also struggled to find food, clean water, and shelter.

The ministry's statement followed an airstrike in the early hours of a residential apartment in western Gaza City. The strike killed two sisters, 15-year-old Yusra, a pupil at Kafr Qasim school, and 13-year-old Jana Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, who attended al-Manar private school. cards.headline: Thirteen people confirmed dead in Bogor, Indonesia, mine flood

pages.text: Thirteen people have died after torrential rain caused a nearby river to overflow and flood two shafts at an open-pit mine in Bogor, Indonesia's West Java province. Authorities confirmed the 13 deaths and the recovery of their bodies from the site. At least 13 more people are thought to still be missing. The disaster occurred on the night of November 23, 2026, while Rais, 50, and at least 25 other miners were digging in the mine, which is approximately 100m (328ft) deep. Small-scale gold mining is banned in Indonesia, but the illegal industry has flourished in rural parts of the archipelago over the last ten years, often correlating with rising gold prices.

Search-and-rescue operations are ongoing as rescuers work day and night to find survivors in the flooded shafts. Personnel are using ropes to access the depths of the dark, narrow, and slippery shafts, which are continually being flooded from below. cards.headline: More than 300 garment factories remain closed in Bangladesh amid labor unrest

pages.text: More than 300 garment factories remained closed on November 26, 2026, as labor unrest continued in the Savar and Gazipur industrial belts on the outskirts of Dhaka, Bangladesh. The closures persist despite the announcement of a new wage structure. In Savar, workers at seven factories stopped work on the morning of November 26, 2026. Mohammad Mominul Islam Bhuiyan, superintendent of Ashulia Industrial Police-1, stated that 22 factories previously declared closed under Section 13(1) of the Labour Act remained shut on that date. In Gazipur, garment workers staged protests at several locations to demand higher wages, disrupting production and causing commuters to take alternative routes to avoid affected areas. Harun Or Rashid, officer-in-charge of Basan Police Station, confirmed that police fired sound grenades to disperse protesters who were attempting to block roads in different parts of the industrial district.

Kazi Ruhul Amin, general secretary of the Bangladesh Garment and Sweater Workers Trade Union Centre, alleged that the new wage structure does not adequately reflect workers' living costs. Amin stated that the nine criteria stipulated in Section 141 of the Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006, were not properly considered when determining the wages and urged authorities to reconsider the pay scale. cards.headline: Alberta legislature passes legislation for new electoral riding maps

pages.text: The Alberta legislature has passed debate on legislation to implement new electoral riding maps, a move that the Opposition NDP says will trigger a legal challenge. The new maps change how provincial electoral districts, or ridings, are drawn, which determines how many people each representative serves and how political power is distributed across the province. The governing United Conservative Party has denied allegations that the changes are designed to provide an unfair advantage in the 2027 election, stating that a special panel was responsible for redrawing the maps and that the changes will boost effective representation.

NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi has alleged the proposed changes favor the United Conservative Party by diluting the power of urban votes. Under the new maps, some urban areas in Calgary and Lethbridge will merge with surrounding rural areas to create hybrid ridings. In Lethbridge, two existing urban ridings are set to become four, consisting of one strictly urban district and three sprawling hybrids that, in some instances, extend to the U.S. border. The government has responded that hybrid ridings already exist in other parts of the province.

The maps include population differences between districts. Urban ridings in Calgary and Edmonton are set to be about six per cent more populated on average than other ridings in the province, while rural ridings are to be consistently underpopulated. The controversy escalated during the fall sitting when Speaker Ric McIver removed deputy NDP leader Rakhi Pancholi from the house for the day after she used the term 'cheating' to describe the government's actions. McIver ruled the term was out of order, while Pancholi stated she was standing up for Albertans.

cards.headline: 31 people killed in massive fire after fuel tanker crashes on Cairo highway

pages.text: At least 31 people were killed and 21 others injured when a fuel tanker overturned and ignited a massive fire on a busy highway in Cairo, Egypt, according to the health ministry. The incident occurred on the evening of November 25, 2026, on a section of a ring road in the Warraq neighbourhood, north of the old city centre. Social media footage showed towering black smoke and flames that torched multiple nearby vehicles. The health ministry dispatched 39 ambulances to the scene, and Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar oversaw the treatment of the injured at a local hospital. The minister noted that the death toll was preliminary and could rise further.

The cause of the crash is subject to conflicting reports and ongoing investigations. State-owned newspaper Al-Ahram reported, citing sources with knowledge of the investigation, that a high-voltage cable fell in front of the private contractor's tanker, causing the driver to lose control, cross the central reservation, and overturn. However, Egyptian prosecutors announced the arrest of a man accused of causing the fire. The prosecution stated the man admitted to speeding when his car collided with the tanker, causing his steering wheel to slip and his car to veer off course. This collision reportedly caused one of the tanker's tyres to explode, leading to the overturn and a subsequent petrol leak that ignited the fire. Regional public prosecutors have launched an investigation and requested DNA samples to identify badly burned victims.

The accident has prompted government action, with Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly ordering an investigation into the causes. A spokesperson for the Egyptian Cabinet stated the government is awaiting full clarification before determining future measures regarding the transport of petroleum products and safety during such operations. This incident follows a pattern of road safety concerns in Egypt, where official figures show nearly 6,000 people died on roads, an increase of several hundred from the previous year's total. Experts attribute frequent collisions to factors such as lax maintenance, speeding, and the flouting of traffic laws. Additionally, Egypt's informal residential areas and run-down infrastructure can complicate emergency responses to large-scale fires.

cards.headline: US judge blocks Trump administration attempt to restrict birthright citizenship

pages.text: A United States federal judge has blocked an attempt by President Donald Trump’s administration to deny birthright citizenship to certain categories of US-born children. In a ruling issued November 25, 2026, District Court Judge Christopher Cooper stated that these children remain under US jurisdiction and are therefore guaranteed citizenship under the US Constitution. This decision follows an August executive order by the Trump administration that targeted birthright citizenship by attempting to deny it to children whose parents were not American citizens or legal permanent residents at the time of the child's birth. The administration argued that the 14th Amendment—which grants citizenship to all persons born or naturalized in the US and subject to its jurisdiction—was not intended to apply to parents who were not permanently living in the country.

The ruling by Judge Cooper in Washington is the second judicial setback for the administration's efforts. In September, another court in Maryland also blocked the policy by issuing a preliminary injunction. To enforce the executive order, the administration will now need to overturn both decisions. This legal battle follows a June ruling by the US Supreme Court, which struck down the president's initial order on birthright citizenship. The Supreme Court ruled that the lawmakers who drafted the 14th Amendment intended for its language to be broad, rather than limited in the manner the president sought. In that June decision, the Supreme Court cited an 1898 case involving Wong Kim Ark, a US-born Chinese American who was denied citizenship because his parents had left the US for China after his birth.

cards.headline: UK number of young people not in education, employment or training falls below one million

pages.text: The number of young people across the UK not in education, employment or training (Neet) fell to 959,000 in the three months to September, according to the Office for National Statistics. While this represents a decrease of 22,000 from the previous period, the figure remains close to the highest level in a decade and is 17,000 higher than the number of 16- to 24-year-olds not earning or learning on an annual basis compared to a year ago. The figure is down from a peak of just over a million in March. This data arrives as Andy Burnham’s government prepares to address a youth jobs crisis following a report by Alan Milburn, which warned that Britain risked “losing a generation of young people” without radical changes to employment support, education policy, and healthcare.

In response to the Milburn report, the government is preparing a full response to his recommendations and intends to publish a white paper on welfare reform. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has promised to create an entirely new welfare system for young people. Work and pensions secretary Pat McFadden stated that the government is fundamentally reforming how it supports young people to invest in their success rather than paying for failure. This follows a parallel review into disability benefits by Labour minister Stephen Timms, who described the existing welfare system as “no longer fit for purpose” and called for significant changes.

cards.headline: Military leaders in Guinea-Bissau delay presidential and legislative elections until November 2028

pages.text: Military leaders in Guinea-Bissau have delayed the country's presidential and legislative elections by two years, pushing back a vote intended to return the West African nation to civilian rule. A decree issued by transitional president Major-General Horta Inta-a stated that the elections, which were initially scheduled for December 6, will now take place in November 2028. The decree cited an “insufficiency of the technical, material and financial conditions” required to conduct the vote. Prime Minister Ilidio Vieira Te also stated that the necessary conditions were not in place for the December elections, though he did not provide a new timeline. This delay follows an army seizure of power that overthrew incumbent Umaro Sissoco Embalo, who was seeking a new term, and disrupted a presidential vote.

The military government, led by former army chief of staff Inta-a, was tasked with overseeing a one-year transition period. A transitional charter published in early December barred Inta-a from running for election. The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), a regional bloc, had called for a short, structured, and transparent transition back to civilian rule. Guinea-Bissau, a country of 2.2 million people, is one of the world’s poorest nations and has experienced coups and attempted coups since gaining independence from Portugal more than 50 years ago. Experts say the country's role as a hub for drug trafficking between Latin America and Europe has fueled its political crises. In August, voters approved a constitutional change that grants the president more powers.

cards.headline: Hong Kong residents hold commemorations for victims of deadly Wang Fuk Court fire

pages.text: Residents in Hong Kong offered flowers and prayers to remember victims of the city's deadliest fire in decades. At a park near the Wang Fuk Court apartment complex in Tai Po, in the north of Hong Kong, people laid flowers, snacks, and toys in tribute. Some residents returned to look at their former homes. A year after the blaze, many survivors continue to adjust to temporary housing, arrange funerals, clean belongings retrieved from charred homes, and determine resettlement plans.

The fire, which occurred on Nov. 26, 2025, engulfed seven high-rise buildings in Wang Fuk Court and killed 168 people while displacing thousands of others. Authorities had previously warned against attempts to exploit the tragedy to stir trouble, and the commemorations were closely monitored. During the tributes, officers from the Civil Aid Service, a government agency, placed many flowers into transparent plastic boxes behind the main flower-laying area, stating the action was to make room as more residents arrived.

The handling of the tributes drew criticism from attendees. Former Wang Fuk Court resident Louis Chan described the officers' actions as disrespectful, and one person in the crowd shouted, “Please have some conscience.” Tim Yu, a 19-year-old student, criticized officers for not answering questions from the public. After night fell, authorities stated that more flowers would be placed in boxes and eventually sent to a Taoist temple, a plan that also drew criticism from residents.

cards.headline: Nigeria seizes over $220 million worth of methamphetamine and arrests five Mexican suspects

pages.text: Nigeria’s National Drug Law Enforcement Agency announced on November 25, 2026, that it seized over $220 million worth of methamphetamine and arrested five Mexican suspects during an operation in Enugu State, in the country's southeast. Agency spokesman Femi Babafemi stated that the suspects, described as “Mexican meth specialists,” were arrested at an industrial-scale laboratory after being under surveillance for weeks. The agency said the Mexicans were allegedly recruited by a Nigerian national and entered the country using forged passports. This operation follows a May bust of a transnational drug syndicate involving Nigerians and Mexicans in southwestern Nigeria.

According to the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency, the suspects were first denied entry into Nigeria in August based on intelligence regarding their alleged plans. They later successfully entered the country by crossing from neighboring Benin using forged passports, though authorities were alerted to their arrival. Operatives monitored the group's movements and activities until their arrest at the Enugu laboratory on November 11. The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime has identified the West and Central Africa region as a major hub for the global trafficking and manufacturing of illicit drugs due to corruption and porous borders.

cards.headline: Myanmar leader refuses to comply with parts of ICJ genocide ruling

pages.text: Myanmar's leader, Min Aung Hlaing, stated that the country will not comply with parts of an International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruling it considers “inappropriate.” Speaking at a meeting on November 25, 2026, the coup leader-turned-president said Myanmar would take actions appropriate for a responsible country but would reject requirements it deems unsuitable, according to state media. Min Aung Hlaing noted that the term “genocide” had seriously affected the country's reputation. The statement did not specify which particular parts of the ruling the government objects to.

The ICJ ruling found Myanmar guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority during a 2017 military crackdown in Rakhine State. The case, which was brought by The Gambia in 2019, centered on military “clearance operations” that resulted in significant violence. The court determined that about 10,000 Rohingya were violently killed during the operation, while approximately 815,000 had been targeted in some way. Additionally, more than 700,000 people are thought to have fled to Bangladesh by foot or by sea. The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of international judges.

Myanmar has denied committing genocide, maintaining that its military forces were responding to attacks by armed groups. Despite these denials, the ICJ found by majority that Myanmar violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention. This decision makes Myanmar the first state to be found in violation of that specific convention. The ICJ is the top United Nations court.

cards.headline: Italian Prime Minister Meloni warns Ukraine against Mediterranean expansion and opposes EU budget proposal

pages.text: Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has warned that the Russia-Ukraine war must not expand into the Mediterranean following a Ukrainian drone strike on a Russian warship and a cargo vessel in the Libyan port city of Benghazi on November 22, 2026. Meloni, a supporter of Ukraine, told reporters in Brussels that while Italy intends to help Ukraine defend itself, the government must also defend the security of its borders and citizens. She stated her intention to be clear about this position with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. This follows a November 25, 2026, interview in which Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said he had spoken with Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Sybiha to stress Italy's commitment to Libya's territorial integrity. The far-right League, another Italian coalition party, also called the attack “unacceptable” and warned it risked destabilizing Libya.

The strike in Benghazi is considered a potentially significant escalation in Ukraine's attacks on Russian interests overseas. In March, Ukrainian sea drones struck and damaged a Russian-flagged tanker carrying liquefied natural gas near Maltese waters. Libya is strategically important to Italy due to direct undersea oil and gas pipelines and operations by the Italian oil company ENI, which runs several fields and terminals in the west of the country. Libya has been divided between two administrations backed by rival foreign powers since a 2011 NATO-backed uprising and civil war toppled Muammar Gaddafi.

Separately, Meloni stated that European Union leaders are far from reaching a deal on a nearly €1.6 trillion ($1.75 trillion) budget proposal for the period of 2028 to 2034. Speaking before an extraordinary EU summit in Brussels, Meloni said, “We’re light-years away from a solution,” and noted that Italy is unwilling to sign off on a budget that requires the country to give more while receiving less. The seven-year budget requires unanimous approval from all 27 member states. Although the budget does not begin until 2028, leaders seek a deal by year-end to avoid complications from upcoming elections in Italy, France, Poland, Greece, Estonia, Finland, and Slovakia.

cards.headline: Digital tool aims to improve healthcare accountability in Taraba, Nigeria

pages.text: A digital tool is being used to help residents in rural Taraba State, Nigeria, hold primary healthcare facilities accountable for how they manage funds. The initiative follows observations of gaps between public health financing rules and actual facility management practices in the region. During a visit to the Primary Healthcare Centre (PHC) in Monkin, Zing Local Government Area, Ahmed Bature, a 27-year-old documentary photographer and government accountability fellow, identified instances where community oversight was being bypassed.

Bature questioned Musa Joel, the chairman of the Ward Development Committee (WDC) at the Monkin facility, regarding how the committee planned to spend its next quarterly Basic Health Care Provision Fund (BHCPF) payment. Joel stated he was unaware the facility had even received a BHCPF payment. Although Joel's signature is legally required before funds can be released from the facility's account, he reported that the officer-in-charge had operated the account for years without informing him of incoming payments or involving him in spending decisions. cards.headline: Illegal mining destroys 560 acres of land and the Pra River in Praho, Ghana

pages.text: Illegal mining, known locally as galamsey, has consumed approximately 560 acres of land in the farming community of Praho in the Akyemansa District of the Eastern Region. The activities have ravaged the environment, destroyed forests and farms, and polluted the Pra River, which serves as the community's main water source. On November 20, 2026, a reporter accompanied by opinion leaders, community youth, and security personnel observed the environmental degradation occurring in the area. The mining operations involve heavy machinery, including bulldozers and excavators, and are reportedly directed by light-skinned foreigners.

The destruction of farmland and water bodies has significantly impacted the livelihoods of Praho residents. Because farming is the community's primary source of income, the loss of land has caused local food prices to rise. For example, cassava that sells for GH¢10 in the regional capital of Koforidua is being sold for between GH¢15 and GH¢20 in Praho. Additionally, the pollution of the Pra River has forced residents to trek almost two kilometres daily to find water for domestic chores, leaving many to depend on rainwater for both farming and household needs.

cards.headline: Scientists discover quasar formed within 630 million years of the Big Bang

pages.text: A German-led team of scientists has discovered the most distant quasar recorded to date. The quasar, which is the core of a galaxy containing a slow-chomping black hole, formed within 630 million years of the Big Bang. This discovery represents a significant advancement in observing the early history of the 13.8 billion-year-old cosmos, as it sets a new record for how far back into the dawn of the universe researchers can see.

Julien Wolf of the European Southern Observatory, who led the study, stated that the discovery represents a major leap in cosmic time. While the previous two records each moved the timeline back by approximately 15 million years or less, this new finding takes researchers back by nearly 40 million years. Wolf described this as the biggest advance in nearly a decade.

cards.headline: Settlers smash foundations of two Palestinian homes in Jaloud, West Bank

cards.headline: Community guardians protect critically endangered southern river terrapins in Malaysia

pages.text: A group of 13 men known as the Terrapin Guardians, or Geng Tuntung, work nightly to protect the nests of the southern river terrapin (*Batagur affinis*) in Terengganu state, Malaysia. The southern river terrapin is listed as critically endangered on the IUCN Red List, a designation indicating the species faces an extremely high risk of extinction in the wild. Working with the Turtle Conservation Society of Malaysia (TCS), the guardians scan riverbanks for heavy shell tracks in the sand to locate nesting sites during the nesting season from January to March. They work from 10 p.m. until dawn to secure nests from natural threats and other collectors.

The community-led conservation program began in 2011. According to TCS data, the guardians have collected and incubated 13,224 eggs and successfully released more than 8,200 young terrapins back into the river. Many of the guardians, including 52-year-old factory production line worker Samsul bin Hamid, previously participated in harvesting terrapin eggs as a seasonal delicacy. Hamid stated that he stopped collecting eggs after learning more about the species through TCS.

cards.headline: Syrian President appoints Kurdish leader Elham Ahmad to People's Assembly

pages.text: Syrian transitional President Ahmed al-Sharaa has appointed senior Kurdish leader Elham Ahmad as a lawmaker, according to an announcement by parliament. The appointment of Ahmad, who formerly headed the Autonomous Administration’s foreign relations department, fills a vacancy for an independent member and brings the total number of members in the People's Assembly from 205 to 206. Four seats remain vacant in the assembly, including three allocated to representatives from Suwayda Governorate where elections have not been held. Under Syria’s current transitional arrangements, Sharaa appoints one-third of the parliament’s members. Sharaa took power after an Islamist group led a coalition that toppled longtime ruler Bashar Assad in December 2024.

Ahmad's appointment formalizes a move previously reported as part of negotiations between the transitional government and the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF). In January, the Kurds and Damascus reached an agreement to integrate Kurdish forces and institutions into the state following a military push by Syria’s new authorities that saw Kurdish fighters relinquish territory seized while battling the Daesh group during the Syrian civil war. In August, Mazloum Abdi, who headed the SDF, announced the dissolution of his Kurdish-led fighting force and was appointed as an adviser to Sharaa. While the integration deal was a major victory for Sharaa, it ended the Kurds’ long-held hopes for official autonomy, a goal Ahmad had fervently pushed for.

Born in Afrin in 1972, Ahmad has played a prominent role domestically and internationally in defending Kurdish rights and advocating for women’s participation in political life. She began her political activism as a women’s rights defender while studying Arabic literature at Aleppo University.

cards.headline: New fossil from South Africa provides clues to the evolution of giant plant-eating dinosaurs

pages.text: A team of vertebrate palaeontologists has described a new dinosaur, *Nyana rooiwalensis*, which lived during the Late Triassic period approximately 210 million years ago. Found in South Africa, the fossil provides new information regarding how sauropodomorphs—the group of animals containing the ancestors of sauropods—evolved into massive herbivores. Sauropods, such as *Brachiosaurus* and *Diplodocus*, are known as long-necked giants that lived 150 million years ago and reached lengths of up to 40 metres and weights of 80 tonnes. These animals did not start at such large sizes; it took millions of years for their ancestors to evolve these gigantic body sizes.

cards.headline: War and access restrictions disrupt olive harvests in Lebanon

pages.text: Lebanon marked World Olive Tree Day as Israeli attacks and restrictions on access to farmland disrupted a fourth harvest season for growers in the south. The disruptions occur amid a national assessment warning that more than a million people across the country are facing acute food insecurity. To mark the occasion, which UNESCO established in 2019, Agriculture Minister Nizar Hani planted an olive tree in the garden of the presidential palace. Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri also planted an olive tree at his official residence in Ain Al-Tineh. President Joseph Aoun described the olive tree as a cornerstone of national identity and a source of income for families, farmers, and artisans from northern Lebanon and the Bekaa Valley to the south and the mountains, calling it a symbol of peace and hope.

Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri accused Israeli forces of uprooting thousands of centuries-old olive trees in occupied border areas, calling the action a violation of international humanitarian law that amounts to a “war crime.” The impact on agriculture has been significant in the South and Nabatieh governorates. The UN Food and Agriculture Organization estimated that 814 hectares of olive groves burned in those governorates between October 2023 and November 2024, resulting in olive production losses of approximately $236 million. A separate Lebanese Agriculture Ministry assessment covering both rounds of fighting estimated production losses at about $307 million, equivalent to roughly 30,700 tonnes of olives, and estimated direct damage to trees at a further $21.5 million. The ministry reported that about 53 percent of farmland in the South and Nabatieh governorates had been inaccessible to farmers at various points due to security conditions.

cards.headline: Brazil President Lula moves to recognize Kapôt Nhĩnore Indigenous Territory

pages.text: President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, known as Lula, has signed a government order recognizing the permanent right of the Mẽbêngôkre (Kayapó) and Yudjá (Juruna) peoples to the Kapôt Nhĩnore Indigenous Territory. The 362,000-hectare (895,000-acre) territory is located on the border between the Pará and Mato Grosso states in the southern Brazilian Amazon. This move is a step toward formal recognition for the two groups, who have been fighting for legal rights to the land since 2004. The territory is the birthplace of Indigenous leader Raoni Metuktire, a prominent defender of the Amazon rainforest. Metuktire has been in palliative care since being diagnosed with cancer at age 94 earlier in 2026.

While the signed ordinance recognizes permanent possession, the territory has not yet achieved full legal recognition. To complete the process, the borders must be marked on the ground, the territory requires final approval by presidential decree, and it must undergo official registration. Only after these steps are completed can authorities remove non-Indigenous occupants. According to data from Brazil’s Indigenous affairs agency, Funai, approximately 83% of the territory still consists of original forest, though the area has been gradually occupied by soy farmers and cattle ranchers.

cards.headline: Funeral home president identified by U.S. as key player in 'Ndrangheta criminal group

pages.text: The U.S. Treasury Department has imposed financial sanctions on a family-owned chain of funeral homes in the Greater Toronto Area, alleging the company's president, 55-year-old Luigi (Lui) Vescio Sr., played a senior role in the 'Ndrangheta. The 'Ndrangheta is a notorious Calabrian criminal syndicate. The U.S. Treasury Department stated that the 'Ndrangheta in the Toronto area has strengthened in recent years, becoming powerful enough to dictate events in Italy from across the ocean. The department further alleged the group in Canada is involved in murder, money laundering, and drug trafficking. Along with Luigi Vescio Sr., the U.S. Treasury Department sanctioned his wife, Rose, and their children, Laura and Luigi Jr., over alleged ties to the syndicate.

Police records obtained by CBC News indicate that Luigi Vescio Sr. has been under investigation by Canadian and Italian authorities for nearly a decade. In 2019, Ontario police captured surveillance images of Vescio meeting with visitors from Italy who were purportedly leading figures in the 'Ndrangheta. Following those meetings, Italian authorities sought Vescio's arrest on a charge of mafia association. The U.S. Treasury Department identified Vescio as a key player in the Canadian wing of the criminal group and named five other men reported to be leaders of the group in the Toronto area, including the purported top boss, Angelo (Don Angelino) Figliomeni.

cards.headline: Brain recordings suggest auditory cortex distinguishes speech from music using basic sound fluctuations

pages.text: A study published in Science Advances suggests the human auditory cortex can distinguish between speech and music by tracking basic pitch and timing fluctuations in sound waves. Researchers used direct recordings from inside the brains of hospitalized patients to reconstruct acoustic patterns, which allowed them to predict when a separate group of listeners heard speech or music, even when the two sounds overlapped. This finding addresses a debate among neuroscientists regarding whether the brain uses dedicated neural modules to categorize abstract sounds like speech and music, or if it relies on tracking the raw physical building blocks of sound waves.

The auditory cortex is a sheet of neural tissue in the brain’s outer layer, located along the upper ridges of the temporal lobes just above each ear. Cells in this tissue respond to spectrotemporal modulations, which are the combined physical patterns of how a sound wave’s energy fluctuates across pitch frequencies and over time. These modulations consist of temporal modulations, which reflect how rapidly loudness rises and falls, and spectral modulations, which describe how closely spaced a sound’s pitch components are. Because of the physics of sound waves, an audio signal cannot pack rapid timing changes and fine pitch spacing into the same instant, providing a physical basis for the brain to separate these categories.

While some brain-imaging studies have identified specialized neural groups in secondary auditory areas that respond selectively to speech, music, or song, other evidence suggests a mix of shared and specialized coding. An earlier brain-recording study of speech and melody listening found generalist temporal-lobe neurons that track pitch across both speech and music, alongside specialized neurons that anticipate upcoming notes in melodies. One perspective holds that much of what appears to be category specialization may grow directly from the physical statistics of sound waves.

cards.headline: Private US non-profit establishes humanitarian corridor in occupied southern Lebanon

pages.text: The American Foundation on Lebanon (Afol), a private US non-profit led by Lebanese-American defense contractor Bilal “Bill” Maadarani, has established a humanitarian corridor within Israeli-occupied southern Lebanon. The organization has provided security escorts and enabled the delivery of humanitarian aid to residents and aid workers in three isolated Christian villages located inside the territory. Afol has also assisted western diplomats and journalists inside the zone on at least two occasions. Maadarani told The National that the organization's goal is to fill critical humanitarian gaps and that Afol is the only organization able to conduct missions without relying on escorts from the UN Interim Force in Lebanon (Unifil). This development occurs as Unifil approaches the end of its mandate and negotiations regarding a replacement for the UN force remain stalled.

The expanding role of Afol has raised concerns among western diplomats, humanitarian workers, and experts. Because the organization is run by a defense contractor, there are worries that private entities could assume functions traditionally held by internationally mandated institutions like the UN, but without equivalent oversight or credibility. One of eight western diplomats interviewed for The National, speaking on condition of anonymity due to diplomatic sensitivity, stated that a UN mandate is essential for European countries and expressed concern that operating without one would allow the balance of power to dictate ground dynamics. Another diplomat emphasized that respecting international humanitarian law must remain a priority. The villages served by Afol are located within a buffer zone that extends 10 to 12 kilometres into Lebanon from the border. Currently, residents in these villages must negotiate military restrictions and secure approvals to leave, with the delivery of essential supplies depending on permission from the Israeli military.

cards.headline: Peel carbon emissions rose 9% in 2025

pages.text: Carbon emissions in Peel increased by 9 percent in 2025, according to a report released by The Atmospheric Fund. The report described the increase as “significant,” noting that the region reached its highest level of emissions in over 10 years. Average per person emissions in Peel rose from 7.1t in 2024 to 7.9t in 2025.

Buildings were the largest contributor to the increase in pollution, with emissions from buildings rising by 14 percent. The report attributed this rise to cold temperatures that increased the demand for gas heating. The second largest contributor was electricity-related consumption, which saw a 24 percent increase in emissions. This was driven by a spike in gas-fired power across Ontario’s grid under the energy policy of the Progressive Conservative government led by Premier Doug Ford. While electricity use in 2025 rose by one percent, the report noted that more power in the province is now being generated from gas.

cards.headline: Women farmers in Uttarakhand, India, are cultivating endangered Himalayan medicinal plants

pages.text: Women living in high-altitude villages in Uttarakhand, India, are working to revive endangered medicinal and aromatic plants (MAPs) through controlled agricultural cultivation. As men often migrate from hill regions for financial opportunities, these women have become central to conservation efforts for species that were previously harvested from the wild. At state fairs across the region, farmers like Guddi Devi are showcasing saplings of these high-altitude plants rather than traditional crops like millet. This shift toward domestication aims to protect species that are facing extinction in their natural habitats due to overexploitation and unsustainable harvesting practices.

The demand for medicinal and aromatic plants has grown significantly, with global exports reaching $4.2 billion in 2023. In the Indian Himalayan region, many of these plants grow at altitudes of 2,000 meters (6,500 feet) or more. Historically, locals traveled up to 100 kilometers (62 miles) on foot to collect herbs such as kutki (Picrorhiza kurroa), which is used to treat fevers, particularly when medical care was difficult to access. However, Guddi Devi noted that because people were digging and harvesting herbs like kutki and sugandha bala (Valeriana jatamansi) from the bugyals—alpine meadows—the species were becoming extinct in those areas, making them difficult to find.

Scientists suggest that moving from wild harvesting to controlled cultivation can provide a sustainable way to meet pharmaceutical demands. Chandra P. Kuniyal, a scientist at the Herbal Research and Development Institute (HRDI), stated that Uttarakhand's diverse agro-climatic conditions make mountain villages located at altitudes of approximately 2,500 to 3,000 meters suitable locations for the domestication and cultivation of these plants. K.S. Kanwal, a scientist at G.B. Pant National Institute of Himalayan Environment, noted that the 'feminization of hill agriculture' is occurring because most men migrate away for work, leaving women to manage these high-altitude agricultural efforts.

cards.headline: New research reclassifies 345-million-year-old Scottish fossil once thought to be an early reptile

pages.text: A 345-million-year-old fossil discovered in Scotland, long regarded as one of the earliest known reptiles, has been identified as a different kind of prehistoric animal. New research published in Nature challenges the specimen's long-established position in evolutionary history. The study was led by scientists from the American Museum of Natural History and the University of Oxford, in collaboration with the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility. The fossil belongs to a species named *Westlothiana lizziae*, nicknamed “Lizzie” due to its resemblance to a lizard. The specimen consists of a nearly complete skeleton preserved within two crushed slabs of rock. For nearly three decades, researchers viewed Lizzie as an important reference point for understanding the evolution of amniotes—a major group of vertebrates that includes reptiles, birds, and mammals. Scientists previously believed the animal was the earliest known amniote adapted to life on land.

The reclassification follows decades of reliance on anatomical features visible only on the fossil's surface. Early descriptions, including the species' scientific description in 1990, focused on four limbs with fingers and toes that appeared to have claw-like tips. These features distinguished *Westlothiana* from many contemporary animals whose limbs more closely resembled fins. However, the fossil's distorted condition made its anatomy difficult to interpret. Xavier Jenkins, a postdoctoral fellow in the Museum's Division of Paleontology and co-lead author of the study, stated that while Lizzie has been an icon for the early evolution of amniotes for decades, researchers found an animal that looked very different from what was expected once they were able to see inside the fossil.
